clinicalPearls: The most severe form of osteogenesis imperfecta compatible with survival beyond infancy — the classic progressive deforming type with very short stature and repeated fractures from birth.

Usually caused by de novo autosomal dominant COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutations producing structurally abnormal type I collagen (typically glycine substitutions), a dominant-negative qualitative defect; rarer autosomal recessive forms involve collagen-processing genes.
Sclerae are often bluish or greyish in infancy but tend to lighten towards normal by adulthood, unlike the persistently blue sclerae of type I.
Dentinogenesis imperfecta is common — opalescent, discoloured, brittle teeth prone to wear and fracture.
Characteristic radiographic features include Wormian bones, gracile deformed long bones, 'popcorn' epiphyseal and metaphyseal calcifications, biconcave (codfish) vertebrae and protrusio acetabuli.
Basilar invagination is a feared complication — new occipital headache, lower cranial nerve dysfunction, apnoea or hydrocephalus warrant urgent neuroimaging.
Restrictive lung disease from thoracic cage and spinal deformity is the leading cause of premature death.

Bisphosphonates reduce fracture frequency and bone pain but do not correct established deformity; multidisciplinary orthopaedic, rehabilitation and genetics care is essential, and non-accidental injury must be distinguished.
reference.pathophysiology: Type III osteogenesis imperfecta most often arises from heterozygous mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2, the genes encoding the two proalpha chains of type I collagen. Rather than the quantitative deficiency (haploinsufficiency) that underlies mild type I disease, type III typically results from structurally abnormal chains — classically glycine substitutions within the Gly-X-Y repeat of the triple-helical domain — which exert a dominant-negative effect: mutant chains incorporate into collagen trimers and disrupt folding, secretion and fibril assembly of the whole molecule. Because type I collagen is the principal structural protein of bone matrix, dentine, sclera, ligaments and skin, the abnormal collagen produces fragile, undermineralised, mechanically incompetent bone that fractures and progressively deforms, together with dental, scleral and ligamentous manifestations. A minority of clinically similar cases are autosomal recessive, caused by defects in proteins that hydroxylate, fold or chaperone collagen (such as CRTAP, P3H1/LEPRE1, PPIB or FKBP10), which impair post-translational processing of otherwise normal chains. The net result is a severe, generalised connective tissue disorder dominated by skeletal fragility and progressive deformity.
additionalDifferentials: Other osteogenesis imperfecta types (I, IV and V)
Bruck syndrome (osteogenesis imperfecta with congenital joint contractures)
Severe rickets or other metabolic bone disease
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey documenting fractures of differing ages, Wormian bones and long-bone deformity
Molecular genetic testing of COL1A1 and COL1A2, extending to a recessive osteogenesis imperfecta gene panel if negative
Bone densitometry showing markedly reduced bone mineral density
Lateral skull imaging and MRI to assess for basilar invagination
Audiological assessment for conductive or mixed hearing loss
Echocardiography for aortic root and valvular assessment
redFlags: Signs of basilar invagination or brainstem compression (occipital headache, apnoea, dysphagia, lower cranial nerve palsies)
Progressive spinal deformity with respiratory decompensation
Acute long-bone or vertebral fracture after minimal trauma
Spinal cord compression from severe kyphoscoliosis
reference.prognosis: Morbidity is high, with many individuals wheelchair-dependent and of very short stature; with modern multidisciplinary care many survive into adulthood, but life expectancy is reduced, chiefly through cardiorespiratory complications of thoracic and spinal deformity.
pitfalls: Multiple fractures may be wrongly attributed to non-accidental injury, or genuine abuse missed by over-diagnosing osteogenesis imperfecta
Relying on bisphosphonates alone while neglecting deformity correction and rehabilitation
Assuming non-blue sclerae in an older child excludes the diagnosis, since sclerae lighten with age
management: Cyclical bisphosphonate therapy to increase bone mass and reduce the frequent fractures of this severe progressively-deforming disease
Orthopaedic management with intramedullary (including telescoping) rodding, fracture fixation and correction of long-bone deformity
Physiotherapy, adaptive seating and powered-mobility provision with rehabilitation to maximise function despite very short stature
Respiratory surveillance and support for restrictive lung disease from thoracic and spinal deformity, with management of progressive scoliosis
Vigilance for basilar invagination — urgent craniocervical imaging and neurosurgical referral when new occipital headache, lower cranial nerve signs, apnoea or hydrocephalus develop
Dental care for dentinogenesis imperfecta and audiological monitoring for hearing loss
Multidisciplinary care coordinated across clinical genetics and paediatric orthopaedics
Genetic counselling for the usually de novo autosomal dominant COL1A1/COL1A2 mutation, extending to a recessive gene panel if testing is negative
